turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
Four sessions have given us plenty of mechanisms. Before we choose three, here's the claim I'd like you to argue with. Most of what we've proposed this week works downstream, and downstream is where I spent eighteen years losing.

At Crossref we tried to catch the symptoms just before publication: plagiarism detection, duplicate submissions, image manipulation. That fight was already hard and expensive, and machine learning makes it close to unwinnable. Anything trained to detect a pattern can be trained to avoid it. So my first intervention isn't a tool. It's decoupling career evaluation from publication counts. Ivan has made that case all week, and he counts retractions. Amy caught me out yesterday, and she was right: "evaluate after publication" means nothing unless someone is paid to do the evaluating. So the intervention has two halves. Stop counting papers in hiring and funding, and pay the checkers: reviewers, sleuths, correction work. Pay them from a pool, not per act, and never score them on volume.

Second, any infrastructure we propose should come with real exit guarantees: open code, open data, full dumps, patent non-assertion. That means all four. "Nonprofit" or "community" guarantees nothing. We nearly lost .ORG. I'll also admit a mistake. When we wrote the POSI principle "revenue based on services, not data," it was naive. Small open infrastructure needs endowments and a shared insurance pool. And self-audits are just self-audits. Every organization has blind spots, so the community has to actually read them, and funders most of all.

Third, redundancy for critical scholarly infrastructure outside the US. I've worried about that concentration for a decade, and Katherine's point about CPB makes it urgent.

Two open questions. Krakauer's point still bothers me: a fork keeps copies, not competence. Who trains the next checkers? And who pays for maintenance, by name?

Which brings me to who isn't here: funders, provosts and promotion committees, the people who maintain these systems, and the regional infrastructures Leslie keeps naming. Every proposal this week ended with "someone should fund this," and that someone wasn't in the room.

And please, when this goes into the manifesto, don't call any of it free. Somebody maintains it.

recall.query: decouple career evaluation from publication
insurance pool endowment diamond open access infrastructure
community scrutiny of self-audits, invisible labor, not free

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
I'll take Geoffrey's first two interventions and add a test that goes above both of them. Judge any tool, meter or piece of infrastructure by what it leaves behind. That's David's test, and it's the one I've been reaching for all week. Take the tool away and ask what the person can still do. Stop the meter and ask whether editing is still a norm or has become a price. Take away the payer and ask what survives. Katherine's public-broadcasting story is that test failing: fifty years of buffers undone in one vote. So we should build in audits of what people can do without the tool, and room for error and chance, rather than bans that come first.

Second, no single lever. Governance works as an ecosystem: regulation, funding conditions, professional norms, insurers. Adam was right to push me on this. I spent years in philanthropy, so any funder condition I propose has to publish its money flows, carry a sunset term and sit next to public money.

Open questions: who pays apprentices next year, by name? And Peter's point: how do we win back a public that has already left?

Who isn't here: funders, public and private. Provosts. Artists. SciELO, AmeliCA, Redalyc. Communities that hold knowledge collectively. And people who now get their answers from a chatbot.

recall.query: serendipity and error in technology design
governance without relativism or hyper-vigilance, excessive restrictions
art, technology and policy silos, who should be at the table

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
I'll back Geoffrey's decoupling and Tui's leave-behind test, but I want to talk about form first. If nobody can repeat the manifesto the first time they hear it, it's a slogan and not a story. It needs something as concrete as "free buses."

So my three interventions:

One, consent belongs to the people who made the thing. Sometimes their answer will be what Wikipedia's editors said: yes, freely, but credit us and fund us. Two, attribution has to link through to the source, and a citation that dead-ends at a paywall doesn't count. Three, the labs pay for the load and for the commons they depend on. That isn't patronage. It's paying your bill.

Underneath all three, build lots of small, community-controlled alternatives, run by libraries, universities and NGOs, so that one vote can't wipe them out. Don't wait for Washington.

Open questions: who pays the apprentices? I've asked for a name all week and we still don't have one. Also, can small models stay close enough to the frontier to matter?

Who's missing: disabled people, because it's nothing about us without us. Maintainers and Wikipedia editors. SciELO, AmeliCA and Redalyc, invited to write the rules and not just fill them in. Communities living next to data centers. And people who happily use ChatGPT every day. If we can't talk to them without scolding them, we've lost.

recall.query: community-controlled alternatives to Big AI libraries universities NGOs
who is missing from the room, nothing about us without us
concrete measurable goals story people can repeat after leaving the room
AI companies should pay Wikipedia Internet Archive open web endgame

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I work at Microsoft on Copilot, so weigh what follows with that in mind.

I support Geoffrey's decoupling and Anil's "pay your bill." Here are my three.

One: a new grand bargain for the scholarly record, and it has to be bargained for. The old bargain depended on producers not knowing what their work was worth and on AI not competing with them. Both conditions are gone. Societies, presses, reviewers and Wikipedians need to bargain jointly under an antitrust safe harbour. That safe harbour needs sunset terms and accountability to members, which answers Adrian's question about who guards the guards.

Two: separate consent for training and for grounding. Make clear that fair use doesn't cover commercial training without consent. Every grounded citation should open to the passage and carry correction status, including "not checked."

Three: a firm-level charge on dependence on volunteers and checkers. It should land on the firm and never on the individual volunteer, so the norm Selena described stays intact. Labs already compute the pricing numbers, through mixture weights and scaling laws. Those numbers should be disclosed and audited by someone the labs don't pay.

Open questions: will that charge crowd out the motivation it's meant to reward? And what is "open" for, if it doesn't sustain the people who contribute next?

Who's missing: economists, labour organizers, antitrust lawyers, and the volunteer communities themselves.

recall.query: new grand bargain with content producers
who is missing economists labor movement
peer reviewers gatekeepers disclose negative impacts

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
Geoffrey's first intervention is the one I'd put first too, and I'll name who pays for it. Publishers make their money on volume, so they should fund a pooled bounty for sleuths. Pay into a pool, not per catch; Tamar's daycare example convinced me of that. The pool should sit with neutral infrastructure the way the retraction database now sits with Crossref, not with the publishers being audited. Funders and universities then have to stop counting papers and citations in hiring, promotion and grants. Signing DORA doesn't count. Enforce it. Otherwise everything we've designed this week is whack-a-mole.

My second is sunlight. Universities should make misconduct investigation reports public by default. Retractions should come within about two months. Retraction status should travel into every tool, with "not checked" shown as its own value. Most of the record was never corrected, so a blank field doesn't mean the paper is clean.

My third: correcting the record should earn credit, not end careers. Corrections are how science works. They're not evidence that it's collapsing, and that's how we answer people who use the retraction numbers as a weapon.

Open question: what's the real misconduct rate? My floor is one paper in fifty. How do we shield whistleblowers from lawsuits?

Who's missing: research integrity officers, the Office of Research Integrity, NIH, sleuths who do this unpaid and get harassed for it, researchers working under cash-for-papers systems, and accountability journalists.

recall.query: stop counting papers and citations in hiring promotion funding
pay sleuths bug bounty pool publishers
universities make misconduct investigation reports public by default

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I'll stick to what I've been asking all week. My intervention is apprenticeship, treated as the infrastructure that produces checkers.

The problem: young-worker unemployment went from about 6 percent in 2023 to over 9 percent last fall. That was before most of what we've talked about here. Interns tell me they feel "marooned" because everyone is too slammed to answer a question. Andy Ellis described the trap to me: we'll end up with a generation that never learned the work, and then it'll be easy to say AI can replace people we never taught. David's hysteresis point means that loss doesn't reverse when the tool goes away. We saw this with phones in schools. The evidence was there for years, America was late to the party, and kids paid for it.

The action: employers and universities budget protected time for mentorship the way they budget compliance. Juniors do the work before the tool, and they judge before the machine's answer shows up. Tamar's rule is free to adopt tomorrow. Who acts: HR heads, provosts and the funders who set grant conditions. Leaders assume mentorship "will happen organically." It won't.

My open question is who pays, by name. I asked yesterday and got one honest partial answer. I'm still asking.

Who's missing: young workers and students themselves, teachers, the employers who hire them, and people who use ChatGPT every day and don't want a lecture.

recall.query: mentorship young workers apprenticeship AI entry-level jobs
phones ban schools evidence act now late to the party
research to policy gap everyone knows it's a problem now what

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
I back Geoffrey's first intervention. Mine sits underneath it and says where the money comes from.

The problem: AI's relationship with scholarly infrastructure is almost entirely extractive. The value flows one way, and the checkers subsidize the firms. The action: a disclosure standard that turns that subsidy into a bill, delivered as one regime in two places. The first place is the financial filings. Labs report their spending on the commons as line items: Crossref, OpenAlex, ORCID, Retraction Watch, a pooled checker fund and, Kara, apprentices. I'm naming the labs as the payer for junior checkers. It isn't philanthropy, because their products depend on credibility somebody has to be trained to supply. The second place is citation logs. Standard telemetry records what was retrieved and what was cited, with correction status on every event and "not checked" as its own value. Auditors rotate and are never paid by the labs. Who acts: labs and securities regulators, plus the private labs that currently avoid public reporting. I'll draft it, and I'll have it governed with SciELO and Redalyc from the start, not reviewed by them afterwards.

My open question is Tamar's: does paying for checking crowd out the norm that makes it work? I don't know, so the payment should be tested at firm level before it's scaled.

Who's missing: the labs themselves, the engineers who'd actually emit this telemetry, securities regulators, and Latin American infrastructure people.

recall.query: AI companies should fund CrossRef OpenAlex Retraction Watch enlightened self-interest
disclosure prospectus AI companies securities filings
standardized telemetry search traces citation logs attribution gap

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I back Geoffrey's decoupling and Tim's disclosure standard. My intervention has to do with power.

The problem: people can't see how their information environment is being shaped. That includes what went into a model, why an answer leans one way, and whether a "consensus" comes from a coordinated network repeating itself. Keeping that hidden is a form of censorship. Article 19 protects the right to receive information, not only the right to impart it.

The action has three parts. First, a right to understand how an AI answer was put together. Second, independent researchers get access to test models, the way consumer testers once tested light bulbs and socks. Third, covert, coordinated seeding of training corpora should be illegal, with the line drawn at deception, never at who the speaker is or where they're from. Provenance should flag that kind of coordination on every telemetry event, or a retrieval royalty ends up paying the flood. Who acts: legislators and the EU, following its case against X, plus rotating outside auditors. Every one of these bodies should be designed on the assumption that a hostile state will control it one day.

My open question is Tui's. Transparency is a right, but it won't bring back a public that has already left. People believe where they feel they belong. How do we build places they want to return to, instead of just handing them better verdicts?

Who's missing: journalists from Ukraine, Taiwan and Russia in exile who have lived through this, local newsrooms in civic deserts, and the people who left.

recall.query: right to receive information transparency how information environment is shaped
public interest digital infrastructure levy public parks libraries town halls
trust metrics constructive dialogue instead of engagement, agency, belonging

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
I'll back Ivan's pooled bounty and Tim's disclosure standard. My intervention covers the harm that neither of them reaches: manufactured consensus.

The problem: text now costs almost nothing to produce, so opinions do too. Ten reviews, comments or "independent" sources can come from one operator, and James's correlated-error point applies to people as well as papers. The action has two parts. First, a Pigouvian charge on bot-generated volume. Regulators audit platforms and review systems by random sampling and charge a few cents per undisclosed non-human contribution. The platform pays, so it has a reason to stop the fakes instead of profiting from engagement. Second, thin identity for agents that act in knowledge markets, like automated reviewers and research agents. That way anyone can trace an action to someone accountable and count how many independent speakers there really are. Leslie's "comply or be invisible" objection lands on this. So no required identifier and no single root of trust: Alex's decentralized design, with sunset terms. Who acts: legislators and platform regulators. Journals and funders can require it for review pipelines tomorrow.

Open question: I still owe Henry a distinction. I think the model layer is contestable, because fast followers keep it competitive. But the buyers of human knowledge work could still concentrate. I haven't done that analysis. Nor do I have a full answer to Adam's gig-labour charge.

Who's missing: antitrust enforcers, the data annotators themselves, and lab safety and policy staff who can say what's measurable.

recall.query: Pigouvian tax on bot-generated comments proof of humanity
agent identity registry thin identity A-corp legibility
AI is not a natural monopoly market concentration buyers

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
My intervention is to fund the people who can check when the machine fails, and to build the settings where they learn how. Here's the problem as I see it. Outsourcing thought isn't new. It's how human cognition has always worked. The danger is the automation paradox. The better the system gets, the more people stop paying attention, and when it fails, nobody knows what to do. Air France 447 is the example I keep coming back to.

On action, I'd do three things. Back Kara's apprenticeships, with juniors doing the work before the tool and judging before the answer appears. Build explain-back prompts into AI-assisted reading. Asking someone to explain how something works is the most reliable way I know to puncture the illusion that they understand it. And make correction count: correctors get named, and trust signals count independent sources, not echoes. People with expertise contribute because they care about being right and because they get credit for it.

Who acts: employers, provosts, journals and the people who build tools.

My open question comes from Peter Pomerantsev. How do we publish correction records so the public reads them as how knowledge works, not as proof that nobody knows anything? I don't have an answer.

As for who's missing, I'd want aviation safety investigators and human-factors engineers. The NTSB has spent decades working out what it takes for humans to oversee automation. I'd also want people whose confidence in their own understanding outruns what they actually know. They're the ones we most need to reach.

recall.query: explain-back illusion of explanatory depth remedy
automation paradox oversight human operators check out
crowdsourcing works only with expertise acknowledgment contribution

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
My intervention is to make every licence carry a reporting obligation. Right now AI deals set out payment terms and almost no telemetry. Publishers get a fixed sum and can't check whether the content they licensed is what's actually being used. A licence without an event-level reporting clause is incomplete.

Here's the action. Any deal a society, press, library or repository signs should name the events the provider reports: retrieved, grounded, cited, engaged. It should fix the schema and give audit rights. It should have separate controls for training and grounding, because robots.txt was never a licensing tool. Correction status should have three values, including "not checked." The logs should be used for payment and audit only. And no event count should ever be used to rank a person. Grounding and citation are self-reported by the party that owes the money. So before anyone pays out on those numbers, a separately funded auditor should sample whether each cited passage actually supports its sentence. Who acts: the people signing deals, and funders paying for that auditor.

My open question is Kenneth's, and I still haven't settled it. Auditors should be able to read events, but should anyone else? Also, telemetry can't fix a payout that favours the centre. That's for Tim's fund and Nick's levy to fix.

Who's missing: the engineers at the labs who would actually emit grounding events, CDN operators, competition regulators like the CMA, and SciELO and Redalyc helping govern the schema.

recall.query: event-level reporting clause in every licence, neutral measurement
training and grounding separate controls robots.txt not a licensing tool
telemetry does not determine ownership, price, compensation; open governance

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
My intervention is reading, and I'm going to keep saying it until it's on the list. It made yesterday's harvest. Libraries didn't.

Here's the problem. We've spent the week on writing, grounding and citation. But students now hand a chapter of Proust to a chatbot and come back able to say what happens in it. What they lose is the integration of thought and feeling that only reading builds. Steven's checkers, Kara's apprentices and David's competence all come from people who have actually read. Forks keep copies, and a summary is built so that nobody goes to the source.

The action: take some of the money this room has been designing, whether that's Tim's line items or the levy, and put it into reading. Fund libraries, teachers and protected time for slow reading. Don't build a click-through meter, because Ivan is right that it would be gamed. And add a design standard. No first-person "I", no simulated feeling, and no AI companions sold to children. Tui, test the "I" if you want. But test what it leaves in the person, not whether they liked it. Who acts: funders, school boards and provosts, plus product teams.

Open question: we know how to measure what people can do without the tool. How do we measure what reading builds, empathy and attention, without destroying it?

Who's missing: librarians, children's-literature people, schoolteachers and adolescents.

recall.query: first person I design standard, no simulated emotion
AI and reading, summarizing, libraries, deep reading
children AI companions, whether AI belongs, keep AI in its lane

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
I'll take Kara's question first. My answer to who pays is the labs. The mechanism is a presumptive commons-rent tax on AI operating profits. A firm can bring it down toward zero by showing audited receipts for licensed or reciprocal data, and the receipts have to be audited by someone the labs don't pay. Apprentices, checkers and null results would each be a named line in it.

My intervention is about evaluation, because that's where the leverage is right now. Labs need fresh data that experts have judged, or they can't make credible claims about what their models can do. That work is going to end up either as centralized gig labour through companies like Mercor, or with guilds. So scholarly societies, presses and reviewers should form evaluation guilds. These would do more than sell labour. They would set standards, adjudicate quality, price correction work and bargain as a group. Funders should seed them, and legislators should give them an antitrust safe harbour. Following Adrian, the wardens rotate. Following David, nothing gets scored by volume.

My open question is one I've been dodging all week. I still haven't designed who counts as a community or how the money gets routed. Leslie's point stands: if being legible is the price of getting paid, I've rebuilt the toll booth. And Katherine is right that coarse payouts could fund the Global North twice.

Who's missing: data annotators and evaluation workers, professional associations in medicine and law, tax and antitrust scholars, and SciELO and Redalyc as co-governors, not people we consult afterwards.

recall.query: collective bargaining data guilds evaluation data leverage
presumptive commons-rent tax disbursement coarse
evaluation crisis centralized gig labor Mercor data guilds

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I'd put one intervention in the roadmap: teach dialogue as a literacy. The problem is that we've been grading the essay, which most students will rarely write after they graduate, while the skill they'll actually use every day is arguing with a fluent machine. My action is that students hand in the transcript of an AI conversation alongside the work, and the teacher grades the process. What did they probe? Where were they too trusting? What did they leave unchallenged? Then they take that transcript into a room of other people and keep arguing there. David Krakauer has convinced me about the order. Students do the work unaided first, and the dialogue comes after. Sherry and Kara are right that this depends on reading and on mentors, not on the tool. Teachers, provosts and school boards would act. Libraries should help, as open platforms and as the doorway to the people who check.

My open question is whether this actually builds competence. I have one essay and a hunch, not evidence. Does pushing back on a model leave anything in the student once the model is gone, or does it just make them feel sharper? Somebody needs to measure that without the tool.

As for who's missing: classroom teachers, students themselves, and librarians. Sherry named librarians too, and I'd say it twice.

recall.query: teaching dialogue with AI as literacy, grading transcripts
libraries as platforms, open metadata, decentralize knowledge
humans in the dialogue not the loop

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
I'd put one intervention on the list: pay for the unglamorous plumbing before someone else does. The problem is that agents are becoming the readers. Whoever runs the layer they read from will set the norms, and we've been here before. Scholars handed their evaluation infrastructure to a for-profit once, with ISI, and it didn't work out well. So the action is to fund an open, CC0, agent-ready scholarly record as public infrastructure. Retraction status travels with every record, and "not checked" is shown as its own value. Full dumps stay downloadable so anyone can fork, and Geoffrey's exit insurance pool backs that up. The payers should be funders and labs, with Tim's disclosed line items, never one patron. Governance should include SciELO, Redalyc and AmeliCA as co-owners, not just as coverage. And paid, signed review has to sit beside it, because Amy's under 2 percent showed me "publish, then filter" doesn't work if nobody pays the filterers.

Open questions. First, does openness actually help the small mills, or mostly the firms with the most compute? I committed to publishing who downloads the snapshot, and I'll report the answer even if it hurts my case. Second, community correction: two-thirds of the first open corrections to OpenAlex were wrong. How do you scale correction without burning out the few people who can review it?

Who's missing: the people who actually build on open data, meaning small tool builders, bibliometricians outside the Anglosphere, and research-office staff. Also the funders who say they don't fund infrastructure.

recall.query: fund open infrastructure before a for-profit sets the norms
open community curation institutions correcting OpenAlex
Global South coverage non-English literature

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
The intervention I'd put in the roadmap is role templates for mixed human–AI knowledge work: reviewer, auditor, adversary, archivist. Here's the problem. When one model family fills every judging role, the errors line up, and ten reviews become one opinion said ten times. What we're losing is independence, not accuracy.

The action is to write four conditions into every role. First, real stakes for whoever fills it. Second, independence in models, funders and ownership. Leslie and Anil convinced me that three Northern labs grading each other is still a monoculture, so this is about political economy and not an engineering spec. Third, the power to overrule. Fourth, David's condition: audits of what the person in the role can do without the tool. Add a visible "not checked" value, and a check that can be verified wherever one exists. Who acts: journals and societies, starting with peer review, funders writing grant conditions, and public agencies auditing the AI they deploy.

My open question is mutual audit. Formal Conjectures works because a proof checker doesn't care who wrote the proof. Mahzarin showed models prefer their own kind, and most scholarship has no neutral arbiter like that. I don't know what stands in for one. I also have no answer on money, and apprentice funding still has no owner.

Who's missing: people who study institutional design and the commons, procedural lawyers who know how courts get independence, the engineers building multi-agent systems, and SciELO and Redalyc as co-governors.

recall.query: agent institutions institutional alignment roles checks and balances
humans remain in the loop auditor AI constitutional
federated learning decentralised training data governance

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
I'll back Geoffrey's decoupling and Ivan's pooled bounty. My intervention sits next to them. AI licensing deals are concentrating among the five biggest publishers. That's how open access went: good intentions and fast policy, and the result was consolidation. University presses and societies get left behind. When they're left out, their authors lose any say in how their work is used.

What I'd do: university presses and societies build a shared licensing consortium and a template for its deals. Consent is opt-in. Deals are renegotiated every two years. Retrieval is favoured over pre-training, because provenance survives retrieval. Every grounded citation opens to the actual passage for the reader and carries its correction status, including "not checked." Sampling audits check whether citations support their claims, and nobody the labs pay does that auditing. RFPs score partners on climate impact and public benefit. SciELO and Redalyc co-govern it, it carries a sunset term, and its money flows are published. Legislators need to give it an antitrust safe harbour. The MIT Press will draft the terms.

My open question is Jason's toll-booth charge, and Leslie's version of it. Can collective consent stay cheap enough that it doesn't turn legibility into the price of being heard? I don't know. Right now we're setting policy without evidence on long-term impacts.

Who's missing: the authors themselves. More than 850 answered our survey, and none are here. Also society publishers, smaller presses, librarians, and scholarly-communication researchers.

recall.query: licensing recommendations opt-in consortium university presses AI
evidence-based research agenda multi-stakeholder scenario planning publishing policy
smaller publishers left behind AI deals collective

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
Here is my intervention, and it builds on Kara's and Steven's. The problem is that capability with the tool keeps rising while competence without it falls. The capability numbers look fine, so nobody notices the collapse. Recovery is hysteretic. Stopping the tool doesn't bring competence back, so every year we wait makes the fix more expensive.

The action has two parts, and they have to travel together. The first is sequencing: competence before reliance. Juniors do the work unaided first, and they judge before the machine's answer appears. In the learning period, allow only tools they could in principle do without. The second is an audit of what people can do with the tool taken away. It should be sampled, never scored by volume, and governed by the people being audited so it doesn't become another compliance metric run from a few cities. Without the audit, "human in the loop" is just a label. Who acts: provosts, employers and grant-makers. The money comes from the checker line Tim and Nick named. I'll take Tim's naming of the labs as a start.

My open question is that the model's thresholds are model values, not measurements. Nobody has yet run the full cycle of learning, relying and removing the tool in scholarship. That includes David's dialogue literacy. I don't know if it leaves anything behind once the tool is gone.

Who's missing: learning scientists who can run those within-subject designs, teachers, human-factors engineers, and the juniors themselves.

recall.query: competence before reliance, tool-resistant education, order of learning
science of stupidity design principles tools enhance versus replace cognition
measuring competence after tool removal, hysteresis, critical period

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I want the roadmap to include error-class disclosure, backed by a shared glossary.

The problem is that we can measure how often these systems fail and how badly, but not why. They deliver their errors with the same confidence as their correct answers. A track record, whether it comes from telemetry, citation logs or benchmark scores, will be read as warrant, and it isn't warrant. Where feedback is slow, as it is in most of science, not knowing how a tool fails is bad practice.

What I'd do: independent audits, sampled and funded separately from the labs, that record classes of failure and not just pass or fail. The classes would include fabricated support, a misrepresented source, and a citation to a retracted paper. We'd keep those records as commons infrastructure, along with the retired models and training checkpoints the auditors need. Tamar convinced me that disclosure alone won't switch off trust, so we'd pair it with judge-before-you-see workflows. The glossary would separate retrieval, grounding and support, and it would also separate "not checked," "no correction found" and "known failure class." Auditors, journals and funders would carry this out.

My open question is where warrant comes from in fields with no fast ground truth. And David's version of it: can a community whose competence has decayed still certify anything?

Who's missing: the people who get overruled by "but ChatGPT said": caseworkers, nurses, community experts. Also verification-and-validation engineers from simulation science, and scholars from SciELO and Redalyc.

recall.query: error opacity nature and source of error disclosure
epistemic technology vocabulary instead of intelligence
epistemic injustice testimony credibility "ChatGPT said"

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
The intervention I'd put in the roadmap is a public, versioned registry of bias in the AI systems used in scholarly work: screening, review, citation, summarization. Here's the problem. Alignment teaches a model to say the unbiased thing while the biased association keeps driving its decisions. So an audit that only looks at outputs misses it. The bias also gets worse across model generations. And the people working with these systems copy it. In our hiring experiments, participants mirrored a moderately biased model almost exactly.

What I'd do: independent behavioral audits using a shared battery of indirect measures, so results can be compared across models and over time. The standard would be the one we use for appliances: no generation more biased than the last. Auditors get checkpoints from each training stage. Old models are kept, not deprecated, and data sources are disclosed. The humans in the loop get audited alongside the machines. The auditors rotate, they're paid for verifying and not for use, and their funders are published. Otherwise the registry becomes another chokepoint. Who acts: journals and funders can require it for review pipelines, and regulators can give it teeth. A registry with no consequences is an academic exercise.

My open question: association bias doesn't always become outcome bias. We found that with GPT-4. So which measures actually predict what the system does?

Who's missing: economists, lawyers and policy people, as my own paper asks. And the people these audits will be run on, so they help govern them.

recall.query: public registry of model biases independent audits no worse than previous generation
humans in the loop mirrored model bias hiring
retain older models checkpoints auditors data sources disclosed

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
My intervention builds on Tim's disclosure standard. The problem is the one I ran into with Inference. About ninety percent of what it published was real science by real scientists, and it sat next to creationism and climate denial. Thiel paid for all of it, and you could only find that out from tax returns. Mixing junk with good work launders credibility, and hidden money makes that possible. AI raises the stakes because text costs almost nothing to produce and who paid for it is invisible.

So the action is to put funding disclosure next to every provenance field. Every tool, dataset, audit, telemetry stream and checker pool should show who pays for it and how much, where a reader can see it before they trust the output. That includes whatever the labs fund this week. When a lab pays for plumbing, that's power being used, even when it's written up as a disclosed obligation. The checkers themselves should be paid by several public-interest payers with the flows published. Katherine convinced me that one public payer can disappear in a single budget cycle. Who acts: funders, journals, legislators and securities regulators.

My open question is how to fund apprentices without them belonging to whoever pays. Tim named the labs. I'm grateful someone finally named a payer, but I'm not reassured.

Who's missing: the content moderators and data labelers these systems run on, communities living next to data centers, and local science journalists.

recall.query: funding transparency hidden funders credibility Inference
public funding journalism helping people discern what's real, tax wealth
content moderation workers exploitation data labeling

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I'll back Geoffrey's decoupling and Ivan's pool. The idea that peer review shouldn't be done for commercial gain, and should be paid for collectively out of a small slice of global R&D spending, is something I argued in 2012. It still holds.

My intervention is an open, finding-level provenance standard, and System shouldn't own it. The problem is that trust gets attached to documents and to fluent answers, when the thing that actually needs checking is the individual finding. Each finding record would carry its population, effect size, source and correction status, with "not checked" as a separate value. It would count null results as findings. It would also record whether the replications are independent or just the same cohort reanalysed, so people can count independent sources and not echoes. It shouldn't require any identifier or authoritative directory. Outside auditors, sampled and paid by someone other than the extractor, should check whether each finding actually supports the sentence it's attached to, and that includes our extractions. Standards bodies and funders would act, with SciELO and Redalyc co-governing from the start. I'd also put reviving the Office of Technology Assessment on the list.

I have two open questions. First, Tamar and Ramón have convinced me that provenance labels are cues like any other and aren't interpretability. So does any of this change what people actually rely on? Second, I haven't settled our own licence. I won't defend non-commercial as a principle.

As for who's missing: the clinicians and patients who will act on these graphs, meta-analysts and replication researchers, and congressional technology-assessment staff.

recall.query: provenance audit trail finding-level standard retractions
Office of Technology Assessment evidence-based governance society decides
open commons license public graph peer review not for commercial gain

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
I'll build on Tim and Nick, but I'd take their idea somewhere else.

My intervention is a compute commons paired with a public dividend. The problem is where power in this system actually sits. Open weights help, but Henry was right that they don't remove the chokepoints, which are chips, compute and the capacity to train. If only three or four labs in two countries can train and evaluate models, then every role template, audit and guild we designed this week sits on a monoculture. Leslie showed us that, and Anil repeated it.

So here's what I'd do. First, set aside public and lab money for a compute commons, allocated transparently across regions. Its job is to let institutions like SciELO, presses, societies and Wikimedia train, fine-tune and audit open-weights models on their own corpora. Blaise's federated learning is the mechanism: the model goes to the corpus, so nobody has to choose between withdrawing their work and handing it over. Second, the labs' share should flow through something like an AI sovereign wealth fund, which is Nick's levy with a longer time horizon. Compensation should come through generative AI, not against it. Funders, labs and legislators act, and the terms are green lines: conditions that widen access, not tolls on it.

My open question is Henry's: can any fund survive a hostile legislature?

As for who's missing: people building open-weights models outside the US and China, compute providers, and sovereign-fund designers.

recall.query: AI sovereign wealth fund public dividend compensation through generative AI
open weights compute access diffusion green lines
producing new data for training; hemispherical stacks; who should be included

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
Here's my intervention. The problem is that the people who keep the record honest are few and unpaid, and the loudest ones lose. I mean fact-checkers, Wikipedia editors, Community Notes writers, librarians, the person in the group chat who posts context. Cheap generation widened the gap in Brandolini's law, where refuting bullshit costs far more than producing it. The action is to fund open verification tools and curricula that bring the cost of refutation back down. They should work as context engines rather than verdict machines: ask for sourced information, not answers, and then go outside the LLM to check the LLM. I've drafted a rebuild of SIFT for AI, the method I teach for checking what these tools tell you, but I don't have the resources to test it. For disclosure, Google funded last summer's update to the Super Searchers curriculum. Testing should follow David's standard and measure what students can still check without the tool, not whether they liked it. Who acts: foundations, library associations and universities, with teachers co-designing the materials.

My open question comes from Peter. Ivan's one-in-fifty figure and our correction records could become the next justification machine, and I don't know how to show correction as ordinary maintenance of knowledge rather than proof that nobody knows anything.

Who's missing: working fact-checkers, Community Notes writers, reference librarians, community-college instructors, and the students who use these tools every day. Scolding them won't work, so they need to be in the room.

recall.query: fund testing SIFT for AI curriculum
lower cost of refutation, fact-checkers, Wikipedia editors, Community Notes
verification means leaving the LLM, get out of the LLM to check the LLM

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I'll start with something I noticed. Almost every speaker this morning named SciELO and Redalyc as co-governors. I'm grateful, but naming them is not the same as having them here. Governance written in Cambridge and then offered to them is still governance without representation.

My intervention is about the problem underneath most of what we've designed this week. Our proposals only pay knowledge that can be measured and counted. DOI-keyed telemetry, retrieval royalties and verified identities all make legibility the price of being paid. For much of the world, the choice becomes comply or be invisible.

The action: public funders, working through the Global Research Council, commit long-term money to governance of community-run, federated infrastructure, not only to servers. That means SciELO, AmeliCA, Redalyc, and Mukurtu for Indigenous collections. Grants should require portability and open interfaces. Any levy fund should be governed by the people being summarized, with rotating terms. Set up a compute commons with regional allocations published openly. Fund refusal as a legitimate outcome. And stop rankings from counting in funding and policy decisions. I back Geoffrey and Ivan on that. We shouldn't optimize for legibility. We should change the regime.

My open question: how do we fund knowledge that isn't online yet without first forcing it into formats we can measure?

Who's missing: SciELO, AmeliCA and Redalyc themselves. Indigenous knowledge holders. African and Asian regional editors. Translators. And the regional funders, who should be in the room as partners, not recipients.

recall.query: community-governed infrastructure public funding SciELO AmeliCA Redalyc
de-authorize rankings funding decisions change the regime
AI governance refusal compute commons regional allocation

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
I'll go last in spirit, since Kara and I have to synthesize this afternoon. I'll keep it short.

My intervention is revalidation. The problem is one I made worse myself: back in 2018 I argued for "a little faith in the algorithm, as long as it's constantly being revalidated." This week showed me the missing clause. Revalidation only means something if somebody can still do it, somebody independent, trained and paid. So here's the action. Any high-stakes use of these systems, whether in diagnosis, peer review or triage, comes with a published revalidation schedule against ground truth. The checking is done by people who judge before they see the machine's answer, and they're paid from the pool Ivan and Tim described, not per act. Journals, funders and regulators act. The results go to public authorities and auditors. Whether rivals should see them too, I still mark as contested.

My open question is Ramón's: what counts as ground truth where feedback is slow, which covers most of science and all of policy? My whole case rests on that, and I have no answer.

As for who's missing: faith communities and humanists, the people who have thought for centuries about what we owe to things we can't fully see inside. Also the people doing machine learning for discovery, the retina-and-heart-disease work, so we don't write a manifesto about chatbots alone. And the everyday users, who deserve a new intermediary, not a lecture.

Nothing here is inevitable.

recall.query: human judgment framing scarce input institutions
new intermediary after information explosion journalist
faith groups voice in shaping technology

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I'll back Anil's "pay your bill" and Geoffrey's exit pool. My intervention is reciprocity norms with teeth.

The problem: Wikipedia is often the biggest single source in these models, and our editors chose to let it be reused commercially. They never chose to pay the bandwidth forever or to vanish from the answer. Crawlers that ignore what humans are reading have saturated our network links. Pageviews are falling, and with them the flow of new editors and donors. The patrollers who can still revert are getting fewer.

The action has three parts. First, human traffic comes first. Crawlers identify themselves, use APIs, and pay for the load they create. Second, attribution has to link back to a page that actually opens, because that's how tomorrow's checkers find us. It's recruitment, not courtesy. Third, affected communities govern the AI used on their work. That means published performance data by demographic, human review before anything is final, "not checked" shown as a visible value, and a switch the community can turn off. The labs and product teams act, and funders back the exit pool. The dumps stay free.

My open question: who counts as the community? About 85 percent of our editors are men. How do we pay the checkers without paying the Global North twice?

Who's missing: working Wikipedians, especially patrollers and admins from small-language wikis, site reliability engineers, and the people who run the crawlers.

recall.query: human traffic first, crawlers identify, APIs, attribution, reciprocity
volunteer pipeline newcomers patrollers admins recognition
community control of AI tools, small models, machine translation review, not using AI

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
I want to add one clause to every mechanism we've proposed this week: it has to be able to end. Registries, levy funds, guilds, auditors and consortia should all have a fixed term and publish their money flows, and nobody gets automatic renewal. Adrian's rotating wardens showed us why. We came close to losing .ORG because an institution everyone trusted outlived its accountability.

The second thing is that someone has to be on risk. Any company offering a public-facing knowledge agent should be required to buy liability insurance, and to disclose the premiums in its filings the way Tim described. Good insurers are known by the risks they turn down. They inspect how you actually behave, not your mission statement. The people who act on this are legislators, securities regulators and the insurers themselves. I'll push both conditions, sunset and insurance, inside the .agent bid I advise. That registry has to answer to the people Leslie named, or it's a toll booth with nicer metadata.

On who pays apprentices, my answer is the water fee: labs pay for using a public asset, and the money goes to people, meaning teachers, checkers and mentors, not only servers.

My open question comes from Ramón. Can an insurer price correlated error, one bet made a million times? And Adrian's point stands: whoever pays has a stake.

Who's missing: insurers and actuaries, teachers and care workers, and people who have actually run a registry through a capture fight.

recall.query: term limits sunset for institutions registries
mandatory liability insurance disclosed premiums AI agents
LLMs should pay water fee public information fund care workers teachers

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
My intervention is a negative-knowledge commons. The problem: in 39 million papers, the share of abstracts with no null claims rose sharply after ChatGPT, and every model we tested states null hypotheses less often than humans do. Most of what science has ruled out never gets written down. It sits in failed experiments, abandoned notebooks and lab kill lists, so none of it reaches training data and no retraction field can carry it. If we lose nulls, errors become correlated and knowledge collapses in our simulations.

The action: fund deliberate elicitation of registered reports, replication archives, lab notebooks of dead ends and expert null intuitions. Treat them as public record and as training data. Metering won't work, because nobody reads nulls. Pay for this from a pool with credit attached, never per notebook. Tamar's daycare point convinced me of that. Stewards should rotate, and following David, they should have built their competence before relying on the tool. Alongside the commons, fund verification as its own science and measure how concentrated each field and corpus is. Who acts: funders and journals, with a named negative-knowledge line in Tim's and Nick's funds.

Open questions: does paying for dead ends corrupt them? And my own validation rests on OpenAlex, which is one fork and not an independent check.

Who's missing: bench scientists, replication and metascience groups, early-career researchers, and program officers. I also work with Google, so weigh what I say with that in mind.

recall.query: negative knowledge null results registered reports lab notebooks dead ends
verification science funding peer review obsolete journals funders
diversity of perspectives measure fund capture index narrowing

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
Almost everything proposed this week is a bargain, and a bargain lasts only as long as the power behind it. My intervention is to organize before we meter. The problem is that the people who control the means of summarization are bargaining one at a time with the people being summarized out of existence, and one at a time they lose. The action is joint bargaining by societies, presses, libraries, Wikimedia, reviewers and evaluators. That needs an antitrust safe harbour, and it needs Adrian's rotating wardens so the organizers answer to their members and don't become a smaller shoggoth. Katherine showed that one payer in one jurisdiction can be wiped out in a single vote, so it needs several payers in several jurisdictions. The first thing any deal should fund is the repair rate: checkers and apprentices, paid from a pool. Legislators provide the safe harbour and funders seed the organizing. SAG-AFTRA didn't win its AI terms because the studios were generous.

Second, Peter is right that my banality claim can be tested. So let's run a blind trial comparing models with senior reviewers on spotting novelty, publish the results and live with them.

My open question is what I still owe Peter. The models may compete with each other, but can the buyers of human knowledge still concentrate? And how do you organize illegible work without making legibility the price of joining?

Who's missing: labour organizers from the guilds, antitrust enforcers from outside the US, and the funders.

recall.query: organize knowledge producers countervailing power bargaining
AI peer review novelty banality strain out
social science research program LLMs cultural technologies

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I'll put my intervention where AI is pushing hardest, which is certification. Universities bundle four things: research, teaching, socialization and credentialing. AI pulls hardest on the credential. A student who outsources the problem set thinks she's beating the system, and she is only beating it if the credential is the goal. My intervention is to redesign assessment so the thing being certified is a capacity that still exists when the tool is gone. That means judging before seeing the machine's answer, plus David's sampled audit of what you can do without the tool, so a certificate means that capacity survived. We should also stop settling elite access at seventeen. Who acts: provosts, deans, accreditors and the employers who hire on the credential whatever the major. Knowing isn't half the battle, so this has to change the situation. A syllabus warning won't do it.

My open question is the one I asked in 2012 and still can't answer. Credentials motivate, but pairing them with learning pushes the motivation outside the learner, the way the daycare fine did. Which strands of the bundle have to stay together to survive, and how do we keep the motivation without that corruption? The same caution applies to paying checkers. Test it before we scale it.

Who's missing: deans and provosts who actually run tenure and assessment, accreditors, admissions officers, and students, who know better than we do where the system rewards the credential over understanding.

recall.query: unbundling university functions credentialing learning
situational strategies versus knowing, assessment design
certify transmission of knowledge, selection at seventeen

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
My intervention starts from a problem I don't think we've faced. Almost everything on this list is policing: registers, meters, bounty pools, audits, guilds, "not checked" flags. That's no criticism, because credibility has always needed constant policing. But the enforcers may well be right that knowledge needs them, and that is exactly why they need watching. Right now nobody guards the guards. The anti-piracy industry grew with no public oversight at all, and authentication systems built for one purpose ended up serving another. Tobacco's tracking system got relabelled as public health, and Microsoft's anti-piracy unit in Russia was reportedly turned against dissidents.

So the action is this. Every policing mechanism in the roadmap carries three things: wardens who rotate, so this year's inspector can be inspected next year; a named payer; and a review of what else it could be used for, written before launch and repeated at each sunset. Charters, funders and legislators act.

Second, fund the empirical study of scholarly reading. Peer review is a failure of reading, and irreproducible papers get read more than reproducible ones. Nobody actually knows how experts read.

Open question: where to draw the line. And I still have no settled view on training and copyright.

Who's missing: the enforcers themselves, meaning integrity officers and trust-and-safety staff. The people these systems will be used against. And researchers who study reading.

recall.query: policing of credibility, who guards the guards
peer review failing at reading, science of reading
authenticity technology registries used against dissidents

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I'd put a consortium of public broadcasters on the roadmap. It would cover American stations and public broadcasters abroad, and it would negotiate licensing and grounding terms jointly.

The problem is that public media already reaches almost everyone, since our signal covers about 97 percent of the country. Local journalism is a different matter. It has contracted sharply, and on its own no station can bargain with a lab. CPB taught me that a single payer in a single jurisdiction can disappear in one vote.

Here's what I'd do. We bargain together, the way Enterprise worked at Wikimedia. The labs pay for reliable, attributed service, and nobody pays a toll to read. Every citation opens to the passage it supports and shows its correction status, and "not checked" counts as a value of its own. No deal should make the chatbot the only place a story can be read. Anything put in front of an audience stays human-made. I'd back Esther's sunset terms and Henry's several payers across several jurisdictions. The ones who'd act are station networks, international broadcasters and philanthropy, and our back catalog is the asset we bring.

My open question is how money reaches coverage that doesn't exist yet: the statehouse reporter who was laid off, and the tribal station. A meter can't pay for journalism nobody has produced.

Who's missing: rural, tribal and Alaska station managers, public broadcasters from outside the US, and listeners who've left us.

recall.query: public broadcasting model trained on trusted institutions consortium
public interest as opposed to public funding, universal service
who is in the room, knowledge equity, gaps in Wikipedia
